articles.title: Social media algorithms on X promote content that conflicts with your values
articles.summary: A new study reveals that X's recommendation algorithm actively promotes content that conflicts with users' personal values. This mismatch is driven by users arguing with posts they dislike, creating a frustrating feedback loop that disproportionately affects left-leaning users.

articles.title: Pixels over Symbols: Sensory Realism Improves Behavioral Alignment in Models of Cognition
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational models of cognition have traditionally relied on abstract symbolic inputs that approximate sensory experiences with simplified vector representations. This simplification reflects historical computational constraints and a long-held assumption that the details of sensory realism are incidental to the study of cognitive processes. articles.title: NeuroHorizon: Long-Horizon Forecasting of Neural Population Activity with Hierarchical Memory
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity tests whether a model has captured dynamics that remain predictive well beyond the observed history. Prediction quality typically declines as the horizon grows, yet neither short-horizon accuracy nor teacher-forced evaluation, which supplies the true activity preceding each predicted step, reveals how well models sustain predictions from an initial history alone. We compare direct multi-step prediction and autoregressive rollout on spiking recordings across horizons and introduce NeuroHorizon

articles.title: From MNH to the Friedman--Komogortsev Method---which changes improve eye-movement classification?
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.11519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Friedman-Komogortsev Method (FKM) is a rule-based classifier of fixations, saccades, and post-saccadic oscillations in 1000-Hz recordings, developed from the modified Nystr\"om-Holmqvist algorithm (MNH) and used in several recent studies. FKM changes MNH in many ways at once: it centres MNH's Savitzky-Golay filter, adds a position-based test for whether an apparent post-saccadic oscillation continues the saccade, adds rejection tests, and changes several thresholds. We asked which of these changes alter agreement with human classification. Bo

articles.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
articles.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.

articles.title: Leafy greens versus meat: Where your nitrates come from may matter for brain health
articles.summary: Leafy greens and bacon both contain nitrates, but a large Danish study suggests the source may matter. Plant-sourced nitrate was tied to lower dementia rates, while animal and tap water nitrate was tied to higher rates.

articles.summary: Women who use social media more often tend to be more open to sugar relationships, according to a study of 22,292 women in 22 countries. The link was modestly stronger in countries with looser social norms.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.

articles.title: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
articles.summary: A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults suggests that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The surprising findings raise the possibility that medications already used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction
articles.summary: A study of more than 17,700 US adults found that people who use cannabis in multiple forms have dramatically higher rates of daily consumption and addiction symptoms than those who stick primarily to one method. Nearly 67% of those who used almost every form met criteria for cannabis use disorder, compared with just 15% of people who mainly consumed edibles.

articles.title: Psychology’s tools for measuring masculinity lean heavily toward the negative, review finds
articles.summary: Is psychology only looking for problems when it studies men? A review of 50 years of masculinity scales found that 78 percent focused mainly on harms, and many overlooked culture and social context.

articles.title: Don't Blame The Preferences: Examining The Emergence of Sycophancy in LLM Training
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI sycophancy, the tendency of large language models (LLMs) to flatter users and affirm their beliefs, can undermine accuracy and contribute to misinformation, dependence, and overconfidence. Although prior work has benchmarked sycophancy in released models and proposed mitigations, its origins during training remain poorly understood. Preference alignment methods such as RLHF and DPO are often blamed, but their effects are rarely compared with earlier training stages.
